evidence_basis.originality_note: All prompts, settings, values and planned diagrams are original. The mapped P2 leaves supply only the demand patterns of pressure subtraction, graph interpretation, density calculation and absolute-pressure distinction. P1 lesson evidence remains deferred.

questions.prompt: A vertical slice of a stationary liquid has cross-sectional area A, vertical height difference Δh and uniform density ρ. Starting from pressure as force per unit area, show why the pressure difference between its lower and upper faces is Δp = ρgΔh.
Two points in the same stationary liquid are 0.20 m and 0.80 m below its surface. What does ρg(0.80 - 0.20) calculate?

options.A: The absolute pressure at the deeper point
options.B: The pressure at the deeper point minus the pressure at the shallower point
options.C: The pressure at the shallower point minus atmospheric pressure in every situation
options.D: The mean absolute pressure of the two points

questions.prompt: The pressure difference between two levels in a liquid is 7.5 kPa and their vertical separation is 0.90 m. Using g = 9.81 m s⁻², which is the best value for the liquid density?

A sealed tank contains a stationary liquid. The gas pressure above the liquid increases by 12 kPa while the liquid density and two sensor depths remain unchanged. What happens to the pressure difference between the sensors?
Two pressure probes are fixed in stationary fresh water of density 998 kg m⁻³. Probe S is 0.50 m below the surface and reads 106.4 kPa. Probe D is 2.30 m below the surface. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the pressure difference p_D - p_S in kilopascals.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Determine the absolute pressure reading at probe D and explain why ρg(2.30 m) should not be added to the reading at S.

questions.prompt: The graph shows the absolute pressure p measured at different depths h in a stationary test liquid. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻².

figure.purpose: Assess separation of the surface-pressure intercept from the hydrostatic gradient.
figure.brief: Original black-and-white line graph of absolute pressure p in kPa against depth h in m. Axes start at h=0 and p=80 kPa. Draw a straight line through exactly (0, 86.0 kPa) and (1.20 m, 98.6 kPa), continuing to 1.80 m. Mark clean grid divisions but do not print the gradient, density or the pressure at 1.80 m.
figure.alt_text: A straight absolute-pressure against depth graph passes through 86.0 kPa at zero depth and 98.6 kPa at 1.20 m.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the pressure at the liquid surface.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Use the graph data to calculate the liquid density.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Determine the absolute pressure at a depth of 1.80 m.

questions.prompt: A research capsule moves vertically through a deep tank of stationary brine with uniform density 1120 kg m⁻³. At point U, 1.40 m below the surface, its absolute pressure sensor reads 118 kPa. At a deeper point L, the sensor reads 154 kPa. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻².

figure.purpose: Provide a spatially clear but answer-safe mixed derivation and pressure-difference problem.
figure.brief: Original black-and-white vertical tank diagram with brine surface, capsule positions U and L, U labelled 1.40 m below surface, readings 118 kPa at U and 154 kPa at L, and an unlabelled vertical bracket between U and L. Do not show the unknown depth, pressure difference, equation or answer.
figure.alt_text: A capsule has two absolute-pressure readings at upper and lower positions in uniform brine.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Use the liquid-column model from the previous lesson to explain why the cross-sectional area of the brine column between U and L does not affect the pressure difference.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the depth of point L below the surface.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Later, an equal 8.0 kPa is added to both absolute sensor readings while the capsule positions and brine are unchanged. State and explain the effect on the calculated depth of L.
